big_idea: Numbers to 200 are made of hundreds, tens, and ones. We can count to 200 by 20s, 25s, and 50s.
learning_intention: We are learning to read and represent numbers up to 200 with base-ten blocks and to count to 200 by 20s, 25s, and 50s.
student_learning_goal: I can read and represent numbers to 200 with base-ten blocks and count to 200 by 20s, 25s, and 50s.
success_criteria: I can build any number to 200 with the right number of hundreds, tens, and ones.
I can read a three-digit number and say what each digit is worth.
I can count to 200 by 20s, 25s, or 50s starting from 0.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart 'Hundreds, Tens, Ones' with three labeled columns

OPTIONAL: Detective Hugo Hundreds (top-hat 'HUNDREDS' badge) — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Three target numbers on the board: 47, 132, 189
0-200 Number Line floor strip rolled out on the carpet
Lesson 1 place-value snapshot tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Detective Hugo found a clue with the number 132 on it. What does 132 actually MEAN? Hugo opens: 'Look at the HUNDREDS first!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Reveal Detective Hugo Hundreds the puppet. 'Friends — meet Detective Hugo. Hugo runs the Place Value Detective Agency. He cracks number cases.' Wiggle Hugo dramatically.

'Hugo's first case is this clue.' Hold up a card with 132 written in large numerals. 'What does this number actually MEAN?'

Take responses. Some children will say 'one hundred thirty-two' (correct reading). Some will say 'one, three, two' (digit naming). Affirm the reading and gently correct the digit naming.

'Hugo says EVERY digit has a JOB. Watch.' Place a place-value mat on the floor. 'This mat has THREE columns. HUNDREDS — TENS — ONES.' Point to each label.

Now build 132 with base-ten blocks. 'Hugo puts ONE hundred-flat in the hundreds column.' Place the flat. 'That digit 1 isn't really 1 — it's 100. THREE ten-rods in the tens column.' Place 3 ten-rods. 'That digit 3 is worth 30, not 3.' 'TWO unit-cubes in the ones column.' Place 2 cubes. 'And THAT 2 is just 2.'

Write on the board: 132 = 100 + 30 + 2. 'See — every digit has a JOB. The job depends on WHERE the digit sits. That's called PLACE VALUE.'

'Hugo says today we'll crack three more cases — 47, 189, and a number Detective Tina found that we'll see soon. AND we'll learn how to skip-count to 200 like detectives following a trail.'
student_actions: Watch Detective Hugo work the case for 132.
Help count the hundreds, tens, and ones for 132.
Predict how 47 will be built (no hundreds, 4 tens, 7 ones).

action.activity_name: Place-Value Cases and the Number-Line Trail

steps.instruction: Whole group: build two more cases on the place-value mat. Case 2: 47 (0 hundreds, 4 tens, 7 ones). Case 3: 189 (1 hundred, 8 tens, 9 ones). For each, write 47 = 40+7 and 189 = 100+80+9. Discuss why 47 has 0 hundreds (children who say 'no zero!' need to see that 0 is a placeholder).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Case 2 — 47. How many hundreds in 47?' Wait. Some children say 0; some say 4. 'Hugo says — 47 is less than 100, so it has ZERO hundreds. The digit 4 is in the TENS place — that's 40. Plus 7 ones — that's 47.' Build it. 'Case 3 — 189.' Build with 1 hundred-flat, 8 ten-rods, 9 unit-cubes.

steps.instruction: Introduce the 0-200 number line. Roll it out on the carpet. 'Hugo says — every detective needs a TRAIL to follow. The Number Line is our trail.' Walk by 20s from 0 to 200 (children take turns hopping each cell). Then 25s (more challenging — 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 175, 200). Then 50s.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Walk the Number Line by 20s — say each number with me.' Walk together: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200. 'Now by 25s — these jumps land on 25, 50, 75…' Children walk and call out. Slow down at the awkward 25s where children might default to 30 (counting by 5s habit). 'Now by 50s — biggest jumps.' 0, 50, 100, 150, 200.

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 minutes each). Station A: Build the Mystery Number — pair draws a number card (e.g., 132, 47, 189, 156, 174, 203 — 203 is a stretch beyond 200), builds with base-ten blocks on the place-value mat, writes the decomposition. Station B: Number Line Trail — pair walks the 0-200 number line skip-counting by 20s, 25s, 50s from various starts. Station C: Hundreds Chart Hunt — pair has a 1-100 chart and a list of numbers; they highlight skip-count patterns by 25s and 50s.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each. Listen for the chime to switch.' Set the rotation. Note: Station A includes one stretch number (203) that can't be built with the available 4 hundred-flats — the pair has to recognise this and report back to the teacher. The recognition itself is meaningful place-value evidence.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the place-value snapshot tracker. Watch for: (a) does the child read the three-digit number correctly (132 not 'one-three-two')? (b) does the child build with the correct number of hundreds/tens/ones? (c) can the child skip-count to 200 by 25s without defaulting to count-by-5s?
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Hand them a number card and ask 'Read this number. Build it. What's each digit worth?' Mark the tracker for reading + building + place-value-naming.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE at Station A: pairs who finish find a SECOND build for 132 (13 ten-rods + 2 ones; or 132 ones). Class compares: same VALUE, different chunks? Cite Fuson (1990) concatenated-single-digit gateway.
steps.teacher_prompt: Hugo: 'Same NUMBER, different CHUNKS. The MATH cares about the TOTAL.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Children whose Grade-1 numbers-to-50 work was emerging stay at Station A (Build the Mystery Number) for both rotations. Limit to numbers under 100 to anchor tens-and-ones first; introduce hundreds only after tens-and-ones is fluent.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch cards: numbers 200-500 (e.g., 273, 408). Discuss whether the place-value rule still applies (yes — extends naturally to hundreds, tens, ones at any scale). Previews Grade 3 territory.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a sentence frame: 'In ___, there are ___ hundreds, ___ tens, and ___ ones.' Provide picture-supported number cards. Pair with a strong-counter peer for Station B (the Number Line walk).
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Number Line Trail at Station B is naturally kinesthetic. Allow movement learners extra rotations there. The body-on-floor walk is the embodied form of skip-counting; for movement learners this is the strongest learning path. NO-MATERIALS PATH: students stand in three carpet lines (HUNDREDS = 100 each, TENS = 10 each, ONES = 1 each); class calls a number and lines step out the right count.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: (1) does the child read 3-digit numbers correctly without digit-by-digit naming? (2) does the child build the number with the correct hundreds/tens/ones counts? (3) can the child skip-count to 200 by 25s and 50s? Children who do all three are at L4 for B1.1 + B1.4.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the place-value snapshot tracker per child as you observe.

discussion_prompts: What's the JOB of each digit in 174?
Why is 132 different from 312, even though they use the same digits?
Which skip-count pattern do you find easiest — 20s, 25s, or 50s? Why?
Can you think of a number from 0 to 200 we use in real life?
Hugo's preview: tomorrow we COMPOSE, DECOMPOSE, and COMPARE 3-digit numbers (Lesson 2 — B1.2). The chunks you built today come back.
consolidation.exit_routine: Hugo's hundreds chant — class chants 3x: Hugo calls 'Look at the HUNDREDS first!' Class: 'Then TENS, then ONES!' Each child writes one 3-digit number with chunk labels.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Three-digit number reading accuracy, build accuracy on the place-value mat, place-value naming, and skip-counting fluency by 20s/25s/50s.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 1 is the diagnostic gateway. Children who confuse 132 with 312 (digit-order issue) need explicit place-value reteach during Lesson 2 small groups. Children who can't yet skip-count by 25s need more 0-200 number-line practice before Lesson 4's estimation work.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child builds 132 as 1 hundred + 3 ones + 2 tens (correct count, wrong placement) — repairing the place-value-as-position misunderstanding
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
Grade-2 children entering 3-digit place value frequently apply a 'concatenated single-digit conception' (Fuson 1990): they read 132 as the digits 1-3-2 without seeing 100+30+2. Ross (1989, 'Parts, Wholes, and Place Value') places multi-digit place value as the primary G2 number-sense gateway; without it, comparison and operations downstream cannot ground.

Today: HUNDRED is a chunk of 10 tens. Tomorrow Lesson 2 composes/decomposes/compares. Lesson 3 even/odd; Lesson 4 estimation; Lesson 5 fair shares.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A (Build the Mystery Number). The child has drawn the card 132. They have placed 1 hundred-flat in the hundreds column, 3 unit-cubes in the ones column, and 2 ten-rods in the tens column. They count: '100, then 100, 110, 120 — 120, then 121, 122, 123. 123!' They look puzzled — the card says 132. The teacher steps in.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Show me what you built. Let's check.' Have the child point to each column. 'Hundreds — 1 flat. Tens — 2 rods. Ones — 3 cubes. So your number is…' The child counts: '100, 110, 120, 121, 122, 123. That's 123.' 'But the card says 132. So something doesn't match.' Pause.

'Let's read the card again. ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-TWO. Where's the THIRTY in your build?' Wait. The child looks. 'Hmm — I have 20 in the tens.' 'Right. THIRTY would be 3 ten-rods, not 2. And TWO would be 2 unit-cubes, not 3. The digits in 132 are 1, 3, 2. They go in HUNDREDS, TENS, ONES — in that order.' Slowly point: 'First digit — HUNDREDS — 1 hundred. Second digit — TENS — 3 tens. Third digit — ONES — 2 ones.'

Have the child rebuild. 'Take everything off. Now build 132 by following the digits in order.' The child places 1 flat, 3 ten-rods, 2 unit-cubes. 'Count.' '100, 110, 120, 130, 131, 132.' 'YES — 132.' Tick 'builds with correct H/T/O counts' on the tracker.

Now set up the practice. 'Try one more. Card 174.' The child reads 'one-hundred-seventy-four'. Asks themselves: 'first digit 1 hundreds, second digit 7 tens, third digit 4 ones'. Builds 1 flat, 7 ten-rods, 4 unit-cubes. Counts. 174. Affirm.

If the child STILL reverses the tens and ones: the digit-to-position mapping isn't yet automatic. Repair by going back to two-digit numbers first. 'Let's go simpler. Card 47.' Build 4 ten-rods, 7 unit-cubes. 'Two digits, two positions — TENS, ONES.' Then add the hundreds back: 'Now 147 — three positions, three digits.' The two-digit anchor stabilises the position-value mapping.

Long-term recovery: provide a place-value mat with explicit position labels at every table for the rest of the unit. The labels are the explicit fix — children learn to read 'HUNDREDS, TENS, ONES' as a fixed sequence that maps to the digits in left-to-right order.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Builds with correct counts but wrong positions; counts the build and gets a number that doesn't match the card. Most common at the start of Grade 2 for transition learners.
(Mid) Recognises the mismatch when the teacher prompts; rebuilds correctly when reminded of the position order; doesn't yet auto-map digits to positions.
(Strong) Reads the number, says 'first digit hundreds, second digit tens, third digit ones', builds correctly without prompting. Has internalised the position-value rule.

(Stretched) Volunteers that 132 is DIFFERENT from 312 because the SAME digits in DIFFERENT positions mean different values. Beginning to articulate place value as a structural property of the number system.
common_misconceptions: The digits go in any order — what matters is that you have all of them. (Position-blindness misconception. Repair: explicit left-to-right reading: HUNDREDS first, then TENS, then ONES.)

The 0 in 'thirty' or 'twenty' isn't a real digit. (Children write 132 but say 'one hundred and thirty-two' as if there's no zero placeholder logic. Repair: connect the spoken word THIRTY to the WRITTEN 30 → 3 tens, not 3 ones.)

More digits = bigger number, no matter what the digits are. (Children compare 99 and 100 by counting digits and getting confused. Repair: show that 100 = 1 hundred = 10 tens; the 1 in 100 isn't 'small' — it's worth a whole hundred.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child reads 132 as '1-3-2': drill the 'hundreds FIRST, tens NEXT, ones LAST' frame; child re-says aloud.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child knows place values but builds wrong (e.g., 13 ten-rods + 2): explicitly accept the alt build but require child ALSO to show 1-100, 3-10s, 2-1s.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child cannot start: drop to 2-digit (32 = 3 tens + 2 ones), establish, then introduce 100s.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of B1.1 (numbers to 200) and B1.4 (skip-counting by 20s/25s/50s). Captures diagnostic-level evidence for the unit.

parts_outline.task: Six base-ten block scenes. Each scene shows a build (e.g., 1 flat + 4 ten-rods + 7 unit-cubes). The child writes the number and the decomposition: 147 = 100 + 40 + 7.
Three Number Line skip-count tasks. Task A: by 20s starting at 0. Task B: by 25s starting at 0. Task C: by 50s starting at 0. Each is a fill-in-the-missing-numbers strip 0-200.
Open prompt: 'In what real-life situations would you see a number bigger than 100? Draw and write.'
